title: Emil of Lönneberga
author: Astrid Lindgren
short_summary: Emil is a mischievous but good-hearted farm boy at Katthult, in the Swedish village of Lönneberga. Every time he gets into one of his scrapes — and there are a great many — his father locks him in the toolshed to think about what he has done. Emil does not mind much: it gives him time to carve another little wooden man, and by now the shelf is getting crowded.
extended_summary:
Emil Svensson lives at Katthult farm around 1900 with his father Anton, his mother Alma, his little sister Ida, the farmhand Alfred and the maid Lina. He is five years old, extremely strong-willed, and entirely without malice — which does not stop him from getting his head stuck in a soup tureen at a party, hoisting Ida to the top of the flagpole, catching his father in a rat trap, or inviting every resident of the poorhouse to Katthult and feeding them the food meant for the relatives.

Each time, his father marches him to the toolshed, and each time Emil sits down and carves another wooden figure. His mother, meanwhile, writes every escapade down in blue notebooks, so that Emil can read about himself when he grows up. The people of Lönneberga eventually get so tired of him that they collect money to send him to America; his mother refuses to take it and tells them Emil is a good boy whom they love.

And when it matters, they are right about him. When Alfred cuts his thumb and the wound turns dangerous just before Christmas, it is Emil who harnesses the horse and drives him through a blizzard to the doctor in Mariannelund — the same stubbornness that causes every disaster in the book, turned to something else.

questions.prompt: What does Emil's mother do about every single one of his escapades?

options: Writes each one down in her blue notebooks
Tells his father the moment he comes in
Makes Emil apologise to everyone involved
Puts his wooden figures away for a week

questions.explanation: Alma keeps a written record so that Emil can read about himself when he is grown up. It is a wonderfully odd thing for a mother to do — she is neither punishing him nor excusing him, she is simply refusing to let any of it be forgotten.

questions.prompt: Emil invites the whole poorhouse to Katthult one day. What is the problem with his hospitality?

options: He feeds them the food meant for the relatives
He does it while his parents are at the church
He promises them beds that the farm does not have
He takes the horse to fetch them without asking

questions.explanation: The generosity is entirely real; it is the arithmetic that is missing. Lindgren keeps doing this — Emil's worst crimes are almost always kind things done at the wrong scale, which is why nobody can stay angry with him for long.

questions.prompt: Every time Emil is shut in the toolshed, he spends the time carving another little wooden ___.
questions.explanation: The shelf fills up steadily through the books, one figure per disaster, and it turns the punishment into a record of its own. By the end of the series the collection runs into the hundreds — and Emil is rather proud of it.

questions.prompt: What does Emil do to his little sister Ida during a party at Katthult?

options: Hoists her to the top of the flagpole
Shuts her in the toolshed and loses the key
Paints her face blue with the laundry dye
Sends her down the well in the water bucket

questions.explanation: Ida, it should be said, enjoys the view. The scene is typical of the books: an action that would be alarming in real life is played entirely for delight, and the person most upset by it is always an adult.

questions.prompt: Put the stages of one of Emil's usual days in the order they happen.

items: Emil has an idea that seems perfectly sensible to him
Something at Katthult goes spectacularly wrong
His father takes him firmly to the toolshed
Emil sits down and carves a new wooden man
His mother writes the whole thing in a blue notebook
By supper everyone at Katthult has forgiven him

questions.explanation: The books run on this loop, and Lindgren never varies it — which is exactly why it is funny. Notice the last step: the forgiveness is as reliable as the disaster, and it is why Emil never becomes frightened of his own family.

questions.prompt: Match each person at Katthult to their part in Emil's life.

right: The farmhand who is Emil's closest friend
The maid who suffers most from his ideas
The little sister who joins in and enjoys it
The one who marches him off to the toolshed

questions.explanation: Four adults and children in one farmhouse, each reacting to the same boy in a completely different way. Alfred is the relationship that matters most: the friendship between a five-year-old and a grown farmhand is what gives the last story its weight.

questions.prompt: Sort each of Emil's actions by how it turns out.

options.label: A head is stuck fast in a soup tureen
A little sister is flying from the flagpole
A father is caught in his own rat trap
The poorhouse is fed until nobody is hungry
A sick farmhand is driven through a blizzard
A horse is brought home from a bad bargain

questions.explanation: The same boy produces both columns, and that is the joke of the whole series. Lindgren never suggests Emil has learned a lesson between them — the daring that puts Ida on the flagpole is the daring that gets Alfred to Mariannelund alive.

questions.prompt: The people of Lönneberga get so tired of Emil that they collect money to send him away to America. What does his mother do?

options: Refuses the money and says Emil is a good boy
Takes the money and buys new tools for the farm
Agrees, and Emil spends a summer with relatives
Asks the villagers to decide the matter by a vote

questions.explanation: It is the moment the books stop being only funny. A whole village has decided that a child is a problem to be exported, and one person refuses the premise — not by arguing that he behaves well, but by saying that he is loved.

questions.prompt: Emil's father shuts him in the toolshed after every escapade — and every time, Emil comes out cheerful, with a new wooden figure. Is that punishment working? Give your reasons.
questions.explanation: Both answers can earn full marks. A strong 'it is not working' answer notices that Emil does exactly the same thing next week and that he rather enjoys the shed. A strong 'it works' answer might argue that it ends the row on the spot, that nobody shouts at Emil for days afterwards, and that he is never afraid of his father. Accept either, with evidence from the book.

questions.prompt: Emil's mother wrote every escapade in a blue notebook so he could read about himself when he grew up. Invent one new Emil escapade for that notebook: what does he set out to do, what goes wrong, and why would his father send him to the toolshed for it?
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong invention follows Lindgren's rule: Emil must be trying to do something sensible or kind, and the disaster must come from the scale of it rather than from spite. An escapade where Emil is simply naughty for its own sake has missed how the books work.

questions.prompt: Emil and his family live on a farm called ___, in the village of Lönneberga.
questions.explanation: Lindgren gives the farm a real geography — a kitchen, a flagpole, a toolshed, a poorhouse down the road — and keeps every story inside it. That is why the sleigh ride to Mariannelund feels so enormous: for once, Emil has to leave.

questions.prompt: Just before Christmas, Alfred's cut thumb becomes dangerously infected. What does Emil do?

options: Drives him through a blizzard to the doctor
Runs to the village to fetch the doctor himself
Hides him in the toolshed and nurses him there
Sends Ida on the horse with a written message

questions.explanation: A small boy harnesses a horse in the dark, in a snowstorm, and takes his friend to Mariannelund because the grown-ups are not going to be in time. It is the same disobedience that fills the rest of the book — and this time it saves a life.
